Chapter 4: Confronting Taboos and Finding Meaning
You know, in today’s world, death is still one of those things almost nobody wants to talk about.
We’ll talk about money, sex, even politics—but when it comes to death? Most people just go silent.
And you really see this in how the funeral industry works. Everything’s polished and neat, designed to keep the gritty reality of death at arm’s length. But for folks who actually work with the dead, there’s just no escaping the truth.
Imagine being the person asked to prepare someone’s body for a final viewing. It’s such an intimate job—one that takes real skill, but also a lot of heart. Families hope to see their loved one looking peaceful, just as they remember them. The staff does all they can, but there’s always this little worry: Will the family find comfort? Or will it all just feel too raw and overwhelming?
Working so closely with death forces people to confront their own fears. Think about it—most of us grow up dreading death, shaped by what we see on TV or in movies, and by a culture that says, “Don’t look, don’t talk about it.” The body becomes something hidden away; dying is treated like the one thing you should never witness.
But in a funeral home, those ideas get challenged, day in and day out.
Then, sometimes, a family wants to do things differently. Maybe they ask for a home funeral, wanting to care for their loved one themselves. This can surprise the staff, but they support it. And yes—it’s messy. It’s emotional. But it’s also deeply meaningful. The family washes and dresses their loved one, sharing stories, tears, even laughter. There’s a closeness there—a sense of connection—that’s often missing from more traditional services.
Here’s something to think about: the taboo around death isn’t just about being scared. It’s also about wanting control. The funeral business is built on the idea that professionals should handle every detail, keeping families “safe” from the messy parts. But sometimes, this just creates distance. It can actually make grief harder, leaving people feeling lost or helpless when it’s time to say goodbye.
Over time, it becomes clear—if we ever want to break this taboo, we need to start talking honestly about death. So, the staff begins having open conversations with families, encouraging questions and helping them choose what feels right. Sure, there’s some pushback. Discomfort. Even anger.
But there’s also relief—a weight lifted just by sharing the burden.
Honestly, working with the dead teaches a powerful lesson about honesty. The taboo is tough, but it’s not impossible to break. With patience and compassion, you really can make space for real conversations, and help people find meaning even in the midst of loss.
The work is tough, no doubt about it. But it’s also incredibly rewarding. Because in facing death together, people often discover a new appreciation for life—a sense of connection that breaks through all the old fears and silence.
